--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Plant Layout and Facility Design ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: - Identify and describe the four basic types of facility layouts - Compare the advantages and disadvantages of each layout type - Apply the steps involved in designing a process layout - Calculate cycle time, theoretical minimum stations, and line efficiency for product layouts - Understand the principles of warehouse and office layout design
Why is Plant Layout Important? Plant layout directly impacts: - **Productivity:** Efficient layouts minimize wasted movement and time - **Cost:** Poor layouts increase material handling costs by 20-50% - **Safety:** Well-designed layouts reduce accidents and injuries - **Flexibility:** The right layout allows adaptation to changing demands - **Employee Morale:** Good layouts improve working conditions
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Types of Facility Layouts There are **four basic layout types**, each suited to different production requirements: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Overview of Facility Layout Types
Layout Type Also Known As Best For Example Industries
Process Layout Functional Layout, Job Shop High variety, low volume Hospitals, Machine Shops, Universities
Product Layout Flow Line, Assembly Line Low variety, high volume Automotive Assembly, Food Processing
Hybrid/Cellular Layout Group Technology, Cell Layout Medium variety, medium volume Electronics Manufacturing, Furniture
Fixed-Position Layout Project Layout Very large or immobile products Shipbuilding, Aircraft, Construction
````` ::: ::: ### Visualizing the Layout Spectrum ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Product Variety vs. Production Volume for Different Layouts](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/layout-spectrum-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Process Layout (Functional Layout) In a **process layout**, similar resources (machines, equipment, workers with similar skills) are grouped together. Work flows between departments based on the specific requirements of each job. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Example Process Layout - Machine Shop](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/process-layout-diagram-1.png){fig-align='center' width=864} ::: ::: ### Characteristics of Process Layouts ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Process Layout Characteristics
Characteristic Description
Equipment General-purpose machines
Labor Skilled workers required
Flexibility High - can handle variety
Processing Speed Slower due to varied routing
Material Handling Higher costs (complex paths)
Scheduling Complex - different routes
Space Requirements Higher - WIP inventory storage
````` ::: :::
Discussion Question: Can you identify a process layout in your daily life? **Think about:** - A hospital emergency room (patients routed based on their needs) - A university campus (students move between buildings for different classes) - A grocery store (customers choose their own path) - A machine shop (parts routed based on required operations) **What makes these process layouts?** Similar functions are grouped together, and "products" (patients, students, customers) follow different paths based on their individual needs.
### Real-World Examples ```{=html}
``` ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Product Layout (Assembly Line) In a **product layout**, equipment and workstations are arranged in a line according to the sequence of operations needed to produce the product. Every unit follows the same path. `````{=html}
Product Layout: Automotive Assembly Line
All products follow the same sequential path
Station 1
Frame
Station 2
Engine
Station 3
Body
Station 4
Interior
Station 5
Wheels
Station 6
Quality
````` ### Characteristics of Product Layouts ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Product Layout: Advantages vs. Disadvantages
Advantage Disadvantage
High production rate High initial investment
Low unit cost Low flexibility
Low material handling Line stops affect all
Simple scheduling Monotonous work
Less WIP inventory Requires balanced workloads
````` ::: :::
Quick Quiz: Product Layout **Question:** A car wash where vehicles move through a series of cleaning stations is an example of which layout type? **Answer:** Product Layout - all cars follow the same path through the same sequence of operations.
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Hybrid Layout (Cellular Manufacturing) **Hybrid layouts** combine the flexibility of process layouts with the efficiency of product layouts. The most common type is the **cellular layout** using Group Technology. ### Group Technology Concept Group Technology (GT) identifies parts with similar characteristics and groups them into **part families**. Machines are then arranged into **cells** to process these families. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cellular Layout with Manufacturing Cells](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/cellular-layout-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: :::
Discussion Question: Benefits of Cellular Manufacturing **What are the main benefits of cellular manufacturing over traditional process layouts?** 1. **Reduced material handling** - Parts stay within the cell 2. **Shorter lead times** - No waiting between departments 3. **Less WIP inventory** - Smaller batches, faster flow 4. **Improved quality** - Workers responsible for complete part 5. **Team accountability** - Cell teams own their output
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Fixed-Position Layout In a **fixed-position layout**, the product remains stationary while workers, equipment, and materials are brought to it. This is used when the product is too large or heavy to move. ### Examples of Fixed-Position Layouts - **Shipbuilding** - Ships built in dry docks - **Aircraft manufacturing** - Large aircraft assembled in hangars - **Construction** - Buildings, bridges, dams - **Surgery** - Patient remains stationary
Challenge Question: Managing a Fixed-Position Layout **What are the unique challenges of managing a fixed-position layout?** Think about: - Scheduling deliveries of materials and equipment - Coordinating multiple contractors/teams - Limited space around the product - Weather and environmental factors (outdoor projects) - Ensuring safety with many workers in one area
--- ## Try it yourself: name the layout Eight facilities. Decide which of the four layout types each one uses. ```{=html}
``` ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Designing Process Layouts Designing an effective process layout involves **three main steps**: ### Step 1: Gather Information You need to determine: - **Space requirements** for each department - **Available space** in the facility - **Closeness relationships** between departments #### From-To Matrix (Load Matrix) A From-To matrix shows the number of trips or loads between departments: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
From-To Matrix: Loads per Day Between Departments
Receiving Machining Assembly Painting Shipping
Receiving - 100 50 0 0
Machining 0 - 200 50 0
Assembly 0 0 - 100 60
Painting 0 0 0 - 150
Shipping 0 0 0 0 -
````` ::: ::: ### Step 2: Develop Block Plans Use the **Load-Distance Model** to evaluate layout alternatives: $$\text{Total Cost} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} L_{ij} \times D_{ij} \times C$$ Where: - $L_{ij}$ = Number of loads between departments $i$ and $j$ - $D_{ij}$ = Distance between departments $i$ and $j$ - $C$ = Cost per unit distance ### Interactive Example: Comparing Two Layouts ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Comparing Two Process Layout Alternatives](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/layout-comparison-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: Teaching demo --- drag the material flow volumes and watch which layout wins. ```{=html}

Load-Distance Calculator

Teaching demo
```
Show the live R code behind this calculator ```{webr-r} #| label: load-distance-calc # Calculate Load-Distance scores for both layouts # From-To data: Receiving->Machining, Machining->Assembly, # Assembly->Painting, Painting->Shipping flow_receiving_machining <- 100 flow_machining_assembly <- 200 flow_assembly_painting <- 100 flow_painting_shipping <- 150 # Layout A distances (linear): all adjacent = 1 unit layout_A_score <- flow_receiving_machining*1 + flow_machining_assembly*1 + flow_assembly_painting*1 + flow_painting_shipping*1 # Layout B distances (compact): most departments closer together # Receiving to Machining = 1.12 (diagonal), Machining to Assembly = 1, # Assembly to Painting = 1.12 (diagonal), Painting to Shipping = 1 layout_B_score <- flow_receiving_machining*1.12 + flow_machining_assembly*1 + flow_assembly_painting*1.12 + flow_painting_shipping*1 if (layout_A_score <= layout_B_score) { cat(sprintf("Layout A (linear) wins by %.1f units\n", layout_B_score - layout_A_score)) } else { cat(sprintf("Layout B (compact) wins by %.1f units\n", layout_A_score - layout_B_score)) } cat(sprintf(" Layout A (linear) %.1f\n", layout_A_score)) cat(sprintf(" Layout B (compact) %.1f\n", layout_B_score)) par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1)) barplot(c(`Layout A (linear)` = layout_A_score, `Layout B (compact)` = layout_B_score), col = c("#2E86C1", "#F39C12"), ylim = c(0, 2400), ylab = "Load-distance score", main = "Lower is better") ```
Why does the linear layout win in this case? In this example, the linear layout (A) wins because the process flow is essentially sequential (Receiving → Machining → Assembly → Painting → Shipping). When flow is **sequential**, a **product layout** (linear arrangement) is more efficient. Process layouts are better when there's **varied routing** between departments.
### Try it yourself: lay out the plant Six departments have to go into a building that is two bays deep and three bays wide. Material moves between them as shown in the flow table. Put one department in each cell; the table works out the distance each flow travels (rows apart plus columns apart) and the total load-distance score. **Lower is better.** Start with the heaviest flows: which pairs of departments must be neighbours? Then check your layout against the best possible score. In class, compare scores: there is more than one way to reach the minimum. ```{=html}
``` ### Step 3: Develop Detailed Layout Once the block plan is selected: - Determine exact sizes and shapes of departments - Plan aisle locations and widths - Consider utilities, safety exits, and accessibility - Use CAD software or 3D modeling for visualization ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Designing Product Layouts (Line Balancing) The key challenge in product layout design is **line balancing** - assigning tasks to workstations to minimize idle time while meeting production requirements. ### Line Balancing Steps 1. **Identify tasks and precedence relationships** 2. **Calculate required cycle time** 3. **Calculate theoretical minimum number of stations** 4. **Assign tasks to stations** 5. **Calculate efficiency** ### Key Formulas **Cycle Time:** $$C = \frac{\text{Available Production Time}}{\text{Desired Output}}$$ **Theoretical Minimum Stations:** $$TM = \frac{\sum t_i}{C}$$ **Line Efficiency:** $$\text{Efficiency} = \frac{\sum t_i}{n \times C} \times 100\%$$ Where: - $C$ = Cycle time - $\sum t_i$ = Total task time - $n$ = Number of workstations ### Interactive Example: Pizza Assembly Line ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Pizza Assembly Tasks
Task Description Time (sec) Predecessors
A Roll dough 40 -
B Spread sauce 25 A
C Add cheese 20 B
D Add toppings 35 B
E Season 15 C, D
F Box pizza 30 E
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Precedence Diagram for Pizza Assembly](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/pizza-precedence-1.png){fig-align='center' width=864} ::: ::: ### Line Balancing Calculation This calculator works through the pizza line in the table and diagram above. It does the three steps from the list at the start of this section, then builds a balanced set of stations for you: 1. **Cycle time** — how often a finished pizza must leave the line to hit the target output. 2. **Theoretical minimum stations** — total task time divided by cycle time, rounded up. No line can do better than this. 3. **Station assignment** — tasks are loaded into stations one at a time, longest eligible task first, never exceeding the cycle time and never starting a task before its predecessors are done. The result gives the actual number of stations and the line efficiency. **What to change.** *Desired output* and *Available time per hour* set the cycle time (60 pizzas/h in 3600 s gives 60 s). Edit the *task times* in the table to see how a slow task, such as the 40 s dough roll, forces idle time elsewhere. The precedence relationships are fixed. Try raising the output until a single task is longer than the cycle time; the line can no longer be balanced without splitting that task or running it on parallel stations. Teaching demo --- change the desired output or the task times and watch the number of stations and the efficiency. ```{=html}

Line Balancing: Pizza Assembly

Teaching demo

Edit the task times. The precedence relationships are fixed.

```
Show the live R code behind this card ```{webr-r} #| label: line-balance-calc # Task data tasks <- data.frame( Task = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"), Description = c("Roll dough", "Spread sauce", "Add cheese", "Add toppings", "Season", "Box pizza"), Time_sec = c(40, 25, 20, 35, 15, 30), Predecessors = c("-", "A", "B", "B", "C,D", "E") ) # Production requirements desired_output <- 60 # pizzas per hour available_time <- 3600 # seconds per hour # Step 1: Cycle time and total work content cycle_time <- available_time / desired_output total_task_time <- sum(tasks$Time_sec) # Step 2: Theoretical minimum stations TM <- total_task_time / cycle_time cat(sprintf("Cycle time %g s per pizza\n", cycle_time)) cat(sprintf("Total task time %g s\n", total_task_time)) cat(sprintf("Theoretical minimum stations %.2f (so at least %g)\n", TM, ceiling(TM))) if (any(tasks$Time_sec > cycle_time)) { cat("!!A single task is longer than the cycle time: split it or use parallel stations.!!\n") } else { # Step 3: Assign tasks to stations (longest eligible task first) preds <- strsplit(gsub(" ", "", tasks$Predecessors), ",") preds <- lapply(preds, function(p) p[p != "-"]) done <- character(0) station <- 0 cat("\nStation assignments:\n") while (length(done) < nrow(tasks)) { station <- station + 1 load <- 0 members <- character(0) repeat { ready <- which(!(tasks$Task %in% done) & sapply(preds, function(p) all(p %in% done)) & load + tasks$Time_sec <= cycle_time) if (length(ready) == 0) break pick <- ready[which.max(tasks$Time_sec[ready])] load <- load + tasks$Time_sec[pick] members <- c(members, tasks$Task[pick]) done <- c(done, tasks$Task[pick]) } cat(sprintf(" Station %d: %s = %g s [idle %g s]\n", station, paste(members, collapse = " + "), load, cycle_time - load)) } # Step 4: Efficiency efficiency <- total_task_time / (station * cycle_time) * 100 cat(sprintf("\nStations used %d\n", station)) cat(sprintf("Line efficiency %.1f%%\n", efficiency)) cat(sprintf("Balance delay (idle time) %.1f%%\n", 100 - efficiency)) } ```
Try It Yourself: Can you find a better balance? **Challenge:** At 60 pizzas/h the total task time is 165 s, so the theoretical minimum is $165/60 = 2.75$, which rounds up to 3 stations. Can the line really be run with 3? **Hint:** Try to fill each station to exactly 60 s. Station 1 must start with A (40 s), and B cannot join it because 40 + 25 = 65 s. **Solution:** No. A alone takes station 1 (40 s). B and D fill station 2 (60 s). That leaves C, E and F, which total 65 s, over the cycle time, so a fourth station is needed. Precedence constraints and indivisible tasks make 4 stations the minimum, for an efficiency of $165/(4 \times 60) = 68.75\%$. Now use the calculator: raise the output to 70 pizzas/h (cycle time about 51 s) or cut the dough roll to 30 s and see how the number of stations and the efficiency respond.
### Extending the Example: The Big-Game-Night Rush The pizzeria runs the line above on a normal night: 4 stations, 4 workers, one pizza every 60 s, so **60 pizzas/h**. On Super Bowl night, Halloween and New Year's Eve the orders pile up at well over 100 pizzas/h. Management has two ways to react, and the question is which one pays. **Part 1: How much more can the line make with extra people?** More workers means more stations, and more stations means each one does less, so the cycle time can drop. The limit is the longest single task. Task A (roll dough, 40 s) cannot be shared between people, so no cycle shorter than 40 s is possible however many people are added: $$\text{Maximum capacity with the line as it is} = \frac{3600}{t_{\max}} = \frac{3600}{40} = 90 \text{ pizzas/h}$$ The card below rebalances the line for the number of workers you pick. It looks for the shortest cycle time at which the same station-assignment rule used above fits the tasks into that many stations. Teaching demo --- step the slider from 3 to 7 workers and watch the cycle time and the station loads. ```{=html}

Part 1: Capacity vs. Number of Workers

Teaching demo
```
Show the live R code behind this card ```{webr-r} #| label: peak-people times <- c(A = 40, B = 25, C = 20, D = 35, E = 15, F = 30) preds <- list(A = character(0), B = "A", C = "B", D = "B", E = c("C", "D"), F = "E") workers <- 4 # Load tasks into stations (longest eligible task first) for a given cycle time assign_stations <- function(times, cycle) { done <- character(0); loads <- numeric(0); members <- character(0) while (length(done) < length(times)) { load <- 0; group <- character(0) repeat { ready <- names(times)[!(names(times) %in% done) & sapply(preds[names(times)], function(p) all(p %in% done)) & load + times <= cycle] if (length(ready) == 0) break pick <- ready[which.max(times[ready])] load <- load + times[pick]; group <- c(group, pick); done <- c(done, pick) } loads <- c(loads, load); members <- c(members, paste(group, collapse = "+")) } list(loads = loads, members = members) } # Shortest cycle time (whole seconds) that fits into the available workers cycle <- max(times) while (length(assign_stations(times, cycle)$loads) > workers) cycle <- cycle + 1 plan <- assign_stations(times, cycle) cat(sprintf("Workers available %d\n", workers)) cat(sprintf("Shortest cycle time %g s\n", cycle)) cat(sprintf("Capacity %.1f pizzas/h\n", 3600 / cycle)) cat(sprintf("Stations used %d\n", length(plan$loads))) cat(sprintf("Efficiency %.1f%%\n", sum(times) / (length(plan$loads) * cycle) * 100)) cat("\nStations:\n") for (i in seq_along(plan$loads)) cat(sprintf(" Station %d: %s = %g s\n", i, plan$members[i], plan$loads[i])) par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1)) barplot(plan$loads, names.arg = plan$members, col = "#2E86C1", ylim = c(0, 100), xlab = "Station (tasks)", ylab = "Station load (s)", main = "Station loads against the cycle time") abline(h = cycle, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#C0392B") if (workers > length(plan$loads)) cat("\n!!Extra workers have nothing to do: task A (40 s) is the bottleneck.!!\n") ```
Step the slider from 4 to 7 workers. With the line as it is, capacity grows from 60 pizzas/h (the balance used earlier) to 80 pizzas/h when the 4 workers are rebalanced. A fifth worker lifts it to 90 pizzas/h. A sixth and seventh add nothing at all, because station A still takes 40 s. **Part 2: Duplicate station A.** To go past 90 pizzas/h, the bottleneck itself must be attacked. Putting a second dough station next to the first (a second roller and a second worker) lets two people roll dough in parallel, so a pizza leaves station A every $40/2 = 20$ s. The next-longest task, D (add toppings, 35 s), now sets the limit: $$\text{Capacity with A doubled} = \frac{3600}{35} \approx 103 \text{ pizzas/h}$$ That costs one more worker (6 in total) and one more piece of equipment. Is a gain of about 13 pizzas/h over Option 1 worth that on the few nights a year when it matters? The cost-benefit card compares the two options for a single rush night and for a year. Only the nights when demand exceeds capacity count as a benefit, so set the *peak demand* to what customers would really order. Your turn --- use the card to find the break-even number of rush nights. ```{=html}

Part 2: Is Duplicating Station A Worth It?

Challenge: Find the number of rush nights per year at which Option 1 (five workers, no new equipment) becomes the better choice. Change only the rush nights; leave every other input at its default.
```
Show the live R code behind this card ```{webr-r} #| label: peak-costbenefit peak_demand <- 110 margin <- 4.5 rush_hours <- 6 rush_nights <- 20 wage <- 20 equip_cost <- 12000 equip_life <- 5 # Capacities from Part 1 and Part 2 base_cap <- 3600 / 60 # normal night: 4 workers, 60 s cycle opt1_cap <- 3600 / 40 # Option 1: 5 workers, rebalanced, cycle limited by A opt2_cap <- 3600 / 35 # Option 2: A doubled (6 workers), cycle limited by D sold <- function(cap) min(cap, peak_demand) night <- function(cap, workers_extra, equip_per_night) { gain <- (sold(cap) - sold(base_cap)) * margin * rush_hours cost <- workers_extra * wage * rush_hours + equip_per_night c(gain = gain, cost = cost, net = gain - cost) } equip_per_night <- equip_cost / equip_life / rush_nights o1 <- night(opt1_cap, 1, 0) o2 <- night(opt2_cap, 2, equip_per_night) cat(sprintf("%-26s %12s %12s\n", "", "Option 1", "Option 2")) cat(sprintf("%-26s %12s %12s\n", "", "5 workers", "A doubled, 6")) cat(sprintf("%-26s %12.1f %12.1f\n", "Capacity (pizzas/h)", opt1_cap, opt2_cap)) cat(sprintf("%-26s %12.1f %12.1f\n", "Pizzas sold per hour", sold(opt1_cap), sold(opt2_cap))) cat(sprintf("%-26s %12.0f %12.0f\n", "Extra margin per night ($)", o1["gain"], o2["gain"])) cat(sprintf("%-26s %12.0f %12.0f\n", "Extra cost per night ($)", o1["cost"], o2["cost"])) cat(sprintf("%-26s %12.0f %12.0f\n", "Net per night ($)", o1["net"], o2["net"])) cat(sprintf("%-26s %12.0f %12.0f\n", "Net per year ($)", o1["net"] * rush_nights, o2["net"] * rush_nights)) d_net <- (o2["net"] - o1["net"]) * rush_nights cat(sprintf("\nDuplicating A beats Option 1 by %.0f $/year\n", d_net)) d_margin <- (sold(opt2_cap) - sold(opt1_cap)) * margin * rush_hours if (d_margin > wage * rush_hours) { cat(sprintf("Break-even: about %.0f rush nights per year\n", equip_cost / equip_life / (d_margin - wage * rush_hours))) } else { cat("!!The extra pizzas do not cover even the extra worker: the second station never pays.!!\n") } ```
Try It Yourself: When does the second dough station pay? **Challenge:** With the default numbers, find the number of rush nights per year below which Option 1 (five workers, no new equipment) is the better choice. Then set *peak demand* to 90 pizzas/h and see what happens to the answer. **Hint:** The extra margin of Option 2 over Option 1 is $(103 - 90) \times \$4.50 \times 6\ \text{h} \approx \$350$ per night. Subtract the extra worker ($\$120$ per night). The equipment costs $\$12{,}000 / 5 = \$2{,}400$ per year, to be recovered from what is left. **Solution:** Each rush night leaves about $\$350 - \$120 = \$230$ after the extra worker. Covering $\$2{,}400$ a year needs $2400/230 \approx 10.4$, so **at least 11 rush nights per year**. With 20 nights the second station earns roughly $\$2{,}200$ a year more than Option 1. If peak demand is only 90 pizzas/h, Option 1 already meets all of it, the extra capacity of Option 2 is never sold, and duplicating A never pays. **Think about it:** The cost-benefit result depends on the margin, the number of rush nights and the demand, not only on the line. What other options could be cheaper than a permanent second station (renting a roller for the day, pre-rolling dough earlier, a pre-made crust on rush nights)?
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Warehouse Layout Design Warehouse layouts are a special case of process layouts focused on **minimizing material handling**. ### Key Principles 1. **Place high-volume items near the dock** 2. **Group items that are often picked together** 3. **Use ABC analysis** for storage assignment: - **A items** (20% of SKUs, 80% of picks): Prime locations - **B items** (30% of SKUs, 15% of picks): Secondary locations - **C items** (50% of SKUs, 5% of picks): Remote locations ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Warehouse Layout: ABC Storage Strategy](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/warehouse-viz-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Office Layout Design Office layouts balance **communication needs** with **privacy requirements**. ### Two Main Approaches ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Office Layout Comparison
Aspect Open Plan Traditional/Closed
Space Shared workspaces Private offices
Walls Partitions/dividers Permanent walls
Flexibility High - easy to reconfigure Low - expensive to change
Communication Excellent Limited
Privacy Low High
Cost Lower Higher
````` ::: ::: ### Office Ergonomics Checklist
Click to expand: Office Ergonomics Best Practices **Posture:** - Support the small of the back - Keep shoulders relaxed - Maintain neutral wrist position - Feet flat on floor or footrest **Lighting:** - Position monitor to reduce glare - Adjust brightness for screen vs. paper work - Use task lighting when needed **Workstation:** - Monitor at arm's length - Top of screen at or below eye level - Keyboard and mouse at elbow height **Work Habits:** - Take breaks every 30-60 minutes - Vary tasks to prevent repetitive strain - Use keyboard shortcuts to reduce mouse use
### The Future of Office Design ```{=html}
``` ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Summary: Choosing the Right Layout ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Layout Selection Decision Guide](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/decision-flowchart-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ### Key Takeaways 1. **Process layouts** offer flexibility for varied products but have higher material handling costs 2. **Product layouts** are efficient for high-volume, standardized products 3. **Cellular layouts** provide a middle ground with benefits of both 4. **Fixed-position layouts** are necessary when products cannot be moved 5. **Line balancing** is critical for efficient product layouts 6. **Warehouse layouts** should minimize travel distance for high-frequency items ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Industry Case Studies ### Case Study 1: Food Processing Plant Layout Food processing facilities have unique layout requirements due to food safety, hygiene, and regulatory compliance. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Food Processing Plant Layout Example](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/food-processing-layout-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1056} ::: ::: **Key Design Principles for Food Processing:** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Food Processing Layout Design Principles
Principle Description Regulatory Reference
Linear Flow Raw materials → Processing → Packaging (no backtracking) FSMA
Zone Separation Physical barriers between raw and ready-to-eat areas HACCP
Cleanability Smooth, non-porous surfaces; rounded corners; proper drainage 3-A Standards
Temperature Control Maintain cold chain; separate refrigerated zones FDA 21 CFR 110
Sanitary Design Handwashing stations, foot baths, air curtains at zone transitions USDA FSIS
Allergen Control Dedicated lines or thorough cleaning between allergen products FALCPA
````` ::: :::
Discussion Question: Cross-Contamination Prevention **Question:** A food processing plant produces both peanut butter products and tree nut-free products. What layout considerations are essential? **Key Considerations:** 1. **Physical Separation:** Completely separate production lines with physical barriers (walls, not just distance) 2. **Air Handling:** Separate HVAC systems to prevent airborne allergen transfer 3. **Personnel Flow:** Dedicated workers for each line, or strict gowning/cleaning procedures when crossing zones 4. **Scheduling:** If shared equipment is unavoidable, schedule allergen products last before deep cleaning 5. **Traffic Patterns:** Forklift and cart paths should not cross between allergen zones 6. **Verification:** Air sampling and surface swabs to verify effectiveness
### Case Study 2: Aerospace Manufacturing Facility Aerospace facilities often use **fixed-position layouts** combined with **process layouts** for component fabrication. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Aerospace Assembly Facility Layout](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/aerospace-layout-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: **Aerospace Layout Characteristics:** - **Clean rooms** for precision components (hydraulics, avionics) - **High-bay areas** for large assembly operations - **Overhead cranes** for moving heavy components - **Flow-line final assembly** (aircraft moves through stations) for high-volume commercial aircraft - **Fixed-position** for military aircraft or low-volume production - **Strict FOD (Foreign Object Debris)** control throughout
Video: Boeing 737 Assembly Watch how Boeing uses a moving assembly line for high-volume aircraft production: ```{=html}
```
### Case Study 3: Automotive Supplier - Hybrid Cell Layout ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Automotive Supplier Facility with Cellular Layout](08-Plant-Layout_files/figure-html/auto-supplier-layout-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: **JIT Delivery Requirements:** Automotive suppliers must often deliver directly to the assembly line in **sequence** (JIS - Just-In-Sequence): ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
JIT/JIS Requirements and Layout Implications
Requirement Typical Standard Layout Impact
Delivery Window ±30 minutes of scheduled time Dedicated shipping lane, staging area near dock
Sequence Accuracy 100% (0 sequence errors) Pick-to-light systems, visual management
Quality Level 0 PPM target (Six Sigma) Inline inspection, mistake-proofing (poka-yoke)

````` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Ergonomics in Manufacturing Ergonomics (human factors engineering) is critical for plant layout design to ensure worker safety, reduce injuries, and improve productivity. ### The NIOSH Lifting Equation The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) developed an equation to evaluate manual lifting tasks: $$RWL = LC \times HM \times VM \times DM \times AM \times FM \times CM$$ Where **RWL** = Recommended Weight Limit (in pounds or kg) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
NIOSH Lifting Equation Factors
Factor Name Formula Description
LC Load Constant 51 lb (23 kg) Maximum weight under ideal conditions
HM Horizontal Multiplier 10/H H = horizontal distance from spine to load (inches)
VM Vertical Multiplier 1 - 0.0075|V - 30| V = vertical height of hands at start (inches)
DM Distance Multiplier 0.82 + 1.8/D D = vertical travel distance (inches)
AM Asymmetric Multiplier 1 - 0.0032A A = angle of asymmetry (degrees)
FM Frequency Multiplier Table lookup Based on lift frequency and duration
CM Coupling Multiplier Table lookup Based on grip quality (good/fair/poor)
````` ::: ::: ### Lifting Index Calculation $$LI = \frac{\text{Actual Weight}}{\text{RWL}}$$ ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Lifting Index Interpretation
Lifting Index Risk Level Action Required
LI ≤ 1.0 Low Task is acceptable for most workers
1.0 < LI ≤ 3.0 Moderate Task poses risk; engineering controls recommended
LI > 3.0 High Task is unacceptable; immediate redesign required

Show the live R code behind this calculator ```{webr-r} #| label: niosh-example-plant # Example: Worker lifts boxes from pallet to conveyor # Conditions: Frequency = 4 lifts per minute, 2 hours; Coupling = Fair (handles present) LC <- 51 # Load constant (lb) H <- 15 # Horizontal distance, hands to ankles (in) V <- 10 # Vertical height at origin of lift (in) D <- 20 # Vertical travel distance (in) A <- 30 # Asymmetry angle (degrees) FM <- 0.72 # Frequency multiplier: 4 lifts/min, 1-2 hours, from NIOSH table CM <- 0.95 # Coupling multiplier: fair actual_weight <- 35 # Actual load weight (lb) # Calculate multipliers HM <- 10 / H # 10 here is a fixed NIOSH constant, not our V VM <- 1 - 0.0075 * abs(V - 30) # 30 = NIOSH's fixed optimal reference height (in) DM <- 0.82 + (1.8 / D) AM <- 1 - 0.0032 * A # Calculate RWL and Lifting Index RWL <- LC * HM * VM * DM * AM * FM * CM LI <- actual_weight / RWL cat(sprintf("Lifting Index: %.2f (RWL = %.1f lb)\n", LI, RWL)) cat(sprintf(" HM (horizontal) %.3f\n", HM)) cat(sprintf(" VM (vertical) %.3f\n", VM)) cat(sprintf(" DM (distance) %.3f\n", DM)) cat(sprintf(" AM (asymmetry) %.3f\n", AM)) if (LI <= 1.0) { cat(" Risk level Low - task is acceptable\n") } else if (LI <= 3.0) { cat(" Risk level Moderate - consider engineering controls\n") } else { cat(" Risk level !!High - immediate redesign required!!\n") } ```
Discussion Question: Reducing the Lifting Index **Based on the example above, what layout or workstation changes could reduce the Lifting Index?** **Solutions (in order of effectiveness):** 1. **Reduce horizontal distance (H):** Move conveyor closer to pallet position - If H = 10": HM improves from 0.67 to 1.0 → RWL increases by 50% 2. **Raise the starting height (V):** Use elevated pallet positions or pallet lifters - If V = 30" (optimal): VM improves from 0.85 to 1.0 → RWL increases by 18% 3. **Eliminate asymmetry (A):** Reposition conveyor directly in front of pallet - If A = 0°: AM improves from 0.90 to 1.0 → RWL increases by 11% 4. **Reduce frequency:** Add a second worker or use automation - If 1 lift/min: FM improves from 0.72 to 0.94 → RWL increases by 31% 5. **Improve coupling:** Use boxes with good handles - If good coupling: CM improves from 0.95 to 1.0 → RWL increases by 5% **Best solution:** Implement a scissor lift for the pallet (adjustable height) and move the conveyor closer. This addresses the largest multiplier reductions.

Problem 1: Layout Selection **Scenario:** A company manufactures custom kitchen cabinets. Each order is unique, with different dimensions, materials, and finishes. Production volume is about 50 units per month. **Question:** Which layout type would you recommend and why? **Answer:** A **process layout** would be most appropriate because: - High product variety (custom orders) - Low production volume - Different operations needed for each order - Flexibility is more important than efficiency
**Problem 2: Line Balancing** **Given:** - Total task time: 240 seconds - Desired output: 30 units per hour - Available time: 3600 seconds per hour **Calculate:** 1. Cycle time 2. Theoretical minimum number of stations 3. If you use 3 stations, what is the efficiency? ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution **Solution:** 1. Cycle time = 3600 / 30 = **120 seconds** 2. TM = 240 / 120 = **2 stations** 3. Efficiency = (240 / (3 × 120)) × 100 = **66.7%**
Problem 3: Warehouse Layout **Scenario:** A warehouse has the following items: - Item X: 500 picks/day - Item Y: 100 picks/day - Item Z: 50 picks/day **Question:** How should these items be positioned relative to the shipping dock? **Answer:** Using ABC analysis: - Item X (high frequency): **Closest to dock** (A zone) - Item Y (medium frequency): **Middle distance** (B zone) - Item Z (low frequency): **Farthest from dock** (C zone)

Question 1: What distinguishes a cellular layout from both process and product layouts? **Answer:** A cellular layout combines characteristics of both: - **From process layout:** Equipment variety within each cell, flexibility to handle part variations - **From product layout:** Sequential flow within the cell, dedicated equipment for part families - **Unique characteristics:** - Parts grouped into families using Group Technology - Cells are self-contained mini-factories - Workers often cross-trained to operate multiple machines - Reduced material handling compared to process layout - More flexibility than pure product layout
**Question 2: Calculate the Lifting Index for the following scenario** **Scenario:** A worker lifts 25 kg boxes from floor level (V=0) to a shelf at waist height. The horizontal distance is 40 cm, vertical travel is 75 cm, no asymmetry, frequency is 2 lifts per minute for 4 hours, and coupling is poor (no handles). **Given multipliers:** - LC = 23 kg - HM = 25/H (H in cm) - VM = 1 - 0.003|V - 75| (V in cm) - DM = 0.82 + 4.5/D (D in cm) - AM = 1.0 (no asymmetry) - FM = 0.65 (from tables) - CM = 0.90 (poor coupling) ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution **Solution:** ``` HM = 25/40 = 0.625 VM = 1 - 0.003|0 - 75| = 1 - 0.225 = 0.775 DM = 0.82 + 4.5/75 = 0.82 + 0.06 = 0.88 AM = 1.0 FM = 0.65 CM = 0.90 RWL = 23 × 0.625 × 0.775 × 0.88 × 1.0 × 0.65 × 0.90 RWL = 23 × 0.625 × 0.775 × 0.88 × 0.65 × 0.90 RWL = 5.7 kg LI = 25/5.7 = 4.4 Risk Level: HIGH (LI > 3.0) - Immediate redesign required ``` **Recommended actions:** Raise starting height (use pallet lifter), reduce horizontal distance, add handles to boxes, reduce frequency.
Question 3: List three Industry 4.0 technologies that impact plant layout design **Answer:** (Any three of the following) 1. **AGVs/AMRs:** Require route planning, charging stations, floor markings, safety zones 2. **Collaborative robots (cobots):** Need safety zones, but smaller footprint than traditional robot cells 3. **Digital twins:** Enable virtual layout testing, reduce physical prototyping 4. **IoT sensors:** Require network infrastructure (5G/WiFi), edge computing locations 5. **AR/VR systems:** Training stations, remote assistance capabilities 6. **Flexible automation:** Modular equipment, quick-connect utilities
Question 4: What are the key differences between food processing plant layouts and general manufacturing? **Answer:** | Aspect | Food Processing | General Manufacturing | |--------|----------------|----------------------| | Flow direction | Strictly one-way (raw → finished) | Can have backtracking | | Zone separation | Physical barriers between raw/clean | Logical separation often sufficient | | Surfaces | Sanitary design, smooth, cleanable | Durability focused | | Temperature | Multiple temperature zones (cold chain) | Generally ambient | | Regulatory | HACCP, FSMA, FDA oversight | OSHA, industry standards | | Allergen control | Dedicated lines or validated cleaning | Not typically a concern | | Traceability | Lot-level required by regulation | Often batch-level sufficient |
Question 5: A warehouse has three product categories with the following pick frequencies. Design the storage zones. **Data:** - Category A: 1200 picks/day, 500 SKUs - Category B: 600 picks/day, 1500 SKUs - Category C: 200 picks/day, 3000 SKUs **Solution:** Using ABC analysis based on pick frequency: - **Category A** (60% of picks, 10% of SKUs): Prime locations closest to shipping dock - **Category B** (30% of picks, 30% of SKUs): Secondary locations, moderate distance - **Category C** (10% of picks, 60% of SKUs): Remote locations, maximum distance from dock **Additional considerations:** - Within each zone, use cube utilization for dense storage of slow movers - Consider pick path optimization (serpentine vs. return routing) - High-frequency items at ergonomic pick heights (waist level) - Reserve space near dock for cross-docking high-velocity items
